items.prompt: A branch office needs encrypted connectivity to a VPC quickly, with moderate and variable bandwidth. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: The branch has an internet connection.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Site-to-Site VPN with redundant tunnels, customer-gateway configuration, routing, encryption parameters, and measured bandwidth and latency limits.
Use Direct Connect because it is always faster to provision than an internet VPN.
Use a public IP route without encryption because the branch firewall provides all privacy.
Use VPC peering directly to the branch because peering terminates IPSec automatically.

feedback.Reason: Site-to-Site VPN uses encrypted tunnels over available internet connectivity and is often suitable for rapid moderate hybrid access.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway terminates IPSec tunnels and exchanges routes with the customer gateway.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect uses both tunnels, chooses static or BGP routing, and tests failover and throughput under realistic traffic.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct Connect requires circuit and provider work, public routing is not encryption, and VPC peering is not a branch VPN.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: VPN is fast to deploy but bandwidth and internet-path variability may not satisfy steady high-throughput SLOs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct Connect generally requires physical or provider provisioning.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A public route does not provide encrypted private connectivity by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC peering connects VPCs and does not terminate branch IPSec tunnels.

items.prompt: A VPN design has two tunnels but both use one customer edge router and one internet circuit. What availability gap remains?
constraints: The customer site has one device.

options.text: Add or evaluate independent customer devices, circuits, and upstream paths where the RTO requires protection from customer-edge or ISP failure, then test each failure separately.
Assume two tunnels eliminate every customer-site failure domain.
Add a third tunnel on the same device and call the site fully redundant.
Use DNS round robin to fail over an IPSec tunnel endpoint.

feedback.Reason: Two VPN tunnels improve tunnel-level resilience but do not isolate a shared customer device or circuit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: VPN tunnels can terminate through separate paths, but all tunnels sharing a router or ISP share that failure domain.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner maps customer-site, provider, and AWS failure domains and exercises each failover path.
Details.errorCorrection: Tunnel count is not device or carrier independence, a third same-device tunnel shares failure, and DNS is not IPSec failover control.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent circuits and devices cost more but are required for site-level resilience.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared customer equipment or ISP failure can drop both tunnels.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A third tunnel on the same device retains the device failure domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS does not negotiate or fail over an IPSec tunnel by itself.

items.prompt: On-premises prefixes change frequently and failover should withdraw a route automatically. Which VPN routing mode should be evaluated?

options.text: Use dynamic routing with BGP where supported, controlling advertised prefixes, route preference, propagation, and failover behavior in both networks.
Use static routes for every prefix and rely on manual updates during an outage.
Advertise every enterprise prefix to every VPC route table without isolation.
Use security groups to withdraw a failed network prefix.

feedback.Reason: BGP can exchange reachability and withdraw failed paths faster than manual static updates for changing networks.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Dynamic VPN routing uses BGP advertisements and withdrawals between the customer gateway and AWS gateway endpoint.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect filters prefixes, sets local preference or AS path policy, and tests tunnel and route convergence.
Details.errorCorrection: Static routes increase operational delay, unrestricted advertisements break isolation, and security groups do not participate in routing.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: BGP reduces manual change but requires routing expertise, filtering, and convergence testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Manual static updates are slow and error-prone for dynamic prefixes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route propagation must respect environment and security boundaries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups filter packets and do not withdraw network routes.

items.prompt: Users in a distant geography experience high VPN setup latency over the public internet. Which feature should be considered?
constraints: The internet path remains the transport.

options.text: Evaluate Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN, comparing its endpoint path, cost, throughput, tunnel behavior, and measured latency against standard VPN.
Assume acceleration makes the VPN a dedicated circuit with guaranteed bandwidth.
Use a public route without IPSec to remove all setup overhead.
Move the customer gateway into AWS without changing the physical path.

feedback.Reason: Accelerated VPN can use the AWS global network path for supported connections but remains an encrypted VPN with service-specific cost and limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Acceleration changes the VPN endpoint path and can improve performance from some locations; it does not turn VPN into a dedicated private circuit.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks tunnel establishment, packet latency, throughput, and failure recovery from actual sites.
Details.errorCorrection: Acceleration does not guarantee dedicated bandwidth, removing IPSec breaks privacy, and a logical gateway move does not move customer traffic.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Acceleration may improve latency but adds processing cost and does not replace Direct Connect for deterministic bandwidth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: VPN acceleration is not a dedicated bandwidth guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unencrypted public routing violates the private connectivity requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Customer-to-AWS physical distance remains unless the network path changes.

items.prompt: A data center sends predictable multi-gigabyte transfers and needs consistent private bandwidth to a Region. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: A provider can deliver a circuit.
The workload still needs backup connectivity.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Direct Connect with a suitable port or hosted connection, virtual interface, DX gateway or Transit Gateway design, and an independent VPN or circuit backup.
Use internet VPN as the only path because encryption guarantees bandwidth stability.
Use VPC peering because it creates a private circuit from the data center automatically.
Use a NAT gateway to obtain deterministic inbound and outbound private bandwidth.

feedback.Reason: Direct Connect is designed for dedicated private connectivity and predictable sustained transfer when provider provisioning is acceptable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A Direct Connect circuit or hosted connection reaches an AWS location and uses virtual interfaces to access VPC or public AWS services.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect sizes ports and optics, chooses DX gateway or Transit Gateway integration, and tests backup routing.
Details.errorCorrection: VPN bandwidth and path vary, VPC peering is VPC-to-VPC, and NAT is not a data-center private circuit.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Direct Connect improves predictable throughput but requires lead time, provider design, and independent resilience.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Encryption does not guarantee stable internet bandwidth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: VPC peering does not connect an on-premises site by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT gateways provide translation for egress, not deterministic hybrid private bandwidth.

items.prompt: An on-premises network needs private IP access to one VPC over Direct Connect. Which interface should be configured?

options.text: Use a private virtual interface associated through the appropriate Direct Connect gateway or VPC path, with BGP prefixes, route filtering, and return routes validated.
Use a public virtual interface because all AWS traffic requires public addressing.
Use a transit virtual interface directly to one VPC without a transit gateway or DX gateway model.
Use a NAT gateway as the Direct Connect virtual interface target.

feedback.Reason: A private VIF carries private connectivity to a VPC or supported gateway association.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Direct Connect virtual interfaces define the VLAN and BGP connectivity type; private VIFs advertise private VPC prefixes through the selected gateway design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator limits advertised networks and confirms symmetric routes from site to VPC.
Details.errorCorrection: Public VIFs reach public AWS services, transit VIFs require a transit gateway path, and NAT is not a VIF target.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Gateway abstraction enables multi-VPC connectivity but requires route and association governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private VPC prefixes use private VIF behavior rather than public AWS service access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Transit VIF requires the corresponding transit gateway and DX gateway architecture.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT gateway translation is unrelated to Direct Connect VIF configuration.

items.prompt: A data center needs private connectivity to Amazon S3 and public AWS service endpoints without sending traffic through the internet. Which Direct Connect path should be evaluated?
constraints: The services use public AWS endpoints.
The organization accepts public AWS service addressing over DX.

options.text: Evaluate a public virtual interface with controlled AWS public prefix advertisements, filtering, and route policy for the required public AWS services.
Use a private VIF for every public AWS service without checking service endpoint behavior.
Advertise 0.0.0.0/0 to AWS and accept every public route without filtering.
Use a NAT gateway in the data center to make Direct Connect public services private automatically.

feedback.Reason: A public VIF is the Direct Connect path for supported public AWS service endpoints and requires careful prefix policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Public VIFs use BGP to access AWS public service addresses over Direct Connect rather than the public internet path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect restricts advertisements and confirms the services and Regions reachable through the VIF.
Details.errorCorrection: Private VIFs serve private VPC paths, unrestricted default routes create risk, and NAT does not change Direct Connect service semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Public VIF can improve path control but demands routing and AWS public-prefix governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private VIF and public AWS service access are different path types.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Broad route advertisements can create unintended traffic paths and security risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT does not automatically make a public AWS endpoint a private service path.

items.prompt: A company needs one Direct Connect connection to reach many VPCs through a Transit Gateway. Which interface and gateway path should be examined?
constraints: A Transit Gateway is the routing hub.

options.text: Evaluate a transit virtual interface associated with a Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway, with route domains, prefixes, and attachment propagation explicitly controlled.
Create one private VIF directly to every VPC on the same connection without gateway associations.
Use VPC peering to make the Transit Gateway unnecessary for all site routes.
Advertise every VPC route to the public internet through a public VIF.

feedback.Reason: Transit VIF and DX Gateway integrate Direct Connect with a Transit Gateway for scalable multi-VPC hybrid routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A transit VIF connects to a Direct Connect gateway, which associates with Transit Gateway and exchanges prefixes under documented limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect controls route propagation and isolation and tests one VPC or attachment failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Private VIF associations are not an arbitrary per-VPC shortcut, peering does not replace the planned hub, and public advertisement is unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized hybrid routing reduces circuits but creates route-domain and shared-gateway governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Scalable multi-VPC routing needs the gateway and VIF model that supports it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Peering does not provide a centralized on-premises route hub for every VPC.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public route advertisement is not a private hybrid design.

items.prompt: A critical site has two Direct Connect links through the same facility. What resilience gap should be reviewed?
constraints: Both links terminate in one location.

options.text: Evaluate independent Direct Connect locations, devices, providers, and circuits, with BGP policy and VPN backup tested against facility and provider failure.
Assume two links in one facility isolate every physical failure.
Use one link and add more VLANs because VLAN count equals circuit redundancy.
Use DNS health checks to move an active Direct Connect circuit to another facility automatically.

feedback.Reason: Direct Connect redundancy must span the physical and provider failures relevant to the RTO.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Multiple VIFs or links sharing a facility, router, provider, or power path share that failure domain.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner designs diverse locations and uses BGP preference or VPN failover with tested convergence.
Details.errorCorrection: Two links in one facility share facility risk, VLANs do not add physical circuits, and DNS does not move layer-3 circuits.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Diverse connectivity costs more but materially improves hybrid availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared facility remains a single physical failure domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: VLANs are logical interfaces and do not equal independent circuits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS is not the routing control for Direct Connect circuits.

items.prompt: A site needs higher throughput from two Direct Connect links. What should be compared?
constraints: Links can terminate in one or more locations.

options.text: Evaluate a Direct Connect LAG with compatible links, LACP, provider and location diversity, aggregate bandwidth, failure behavior, and port limits.
Assume two independent links automatically form one aggregated connection without LACP or provider support.
Use DNS round robin to split one TCP flow across circuits.
Add more BGP prefixes because route count directly increases link bandwidth.

feedback.Reason: A LAG can aggregate compatible Direct Connect links but requires physical, provider, and routing validation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: LAG uses link aggregation protocols and supported connections to present combined capacity, while a single flow may have its own limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates LACP, member failure, traffic distribution, and whether diversity goals remain intact.
Details.errorCorrection: Links do not aggregate automatically, DNS does not split an established TCP flow, and route count does not create bandwidth.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: LAG improves aggregate capacity but may concentrate links in one location unless designed with additional diversity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Aggregation requires compatible LAG and provider configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS cannot split a single established flow across circuits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: BGP route count is not a bandwidth control.

items.prompt: A nightly transfer must complete in one hour and the data volume is known. How should the hybrid link be sized?
constraints: Usable throughput is below line rate.

options.text: Size for the required usable throughput with protocol overhead, encryption, contention, burst headroom, failure capacity, and measured transfer efficiency rather than nominal link rate alone.
Choose a link equal to data volume per hour without overhead or other traffic analysis.
Assume compression always halves the required bandwidth regardless of data shape.
Use latency as the only bandwidth sizing input because high latency means low capacity.

feedback.Reason: Bandwidth sizing converts volume and deadline into usable capacity and includes overhead, contention, and failure headroom.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Protocol, encryption, retransmission, storage, and shared traffic reduce application payload throughput below nominal circuit speed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner load-tests the actual transfer path and reserves capacity for peak and degraded-link operation.
Details.errorCorrection: Nominal rate is not payload rate, compression depends on data, and latency is distinct from throughput.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Overprovisioning costs more but protects deadlines and resilience during link or workload variation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Nominal link rate omits overhead, contention, and headroom.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Compression ratio depends on data and processing behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Latency and throughput are related but not interchangeable sizing inputs.

items.prompt: A VPN application has intermittent large-packet failures while small requests work. Which network issue should be tested?
constraints: Path MTU discovery may be filtered.

options.text: Measure effective tunnel MTU, fragmentation or encapsulation overhead, MSS behavior, PMTUD, and firewall handling, then tune the supported path and application if needed.
Increase packet size because larger packets always improve VPN throughput.
Disable all ICMP because it causes fragmentation problems.
Add a second DNS record to split large packets across tunnels.

feedback.Reason: Tunnel encapsulation reduces effective MTU and can expose failures when fragmentation or path discovery is blocked.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IPSec adds headers and path devices may enforce a smaller MTU; TCP MSS or PMTUD can prevent oversized packets.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator captures or measures packet behavior and adjusts supported MTU or MSS and security rules.
Details.errorCorrection: Larger packets worsen the issue, disabling all ICMP can break PMTUD, and DNS does not split packets across tunnels.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower MTU can reduce payload efficiency but improve reliability through tunnel paths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Larger packets may exceed the effective tunnel MTU.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Some ICMP messages are needed for path discovery and diagnostics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS selection does not fragment or distribute individual packets.

items.prompt: On-premises clients need to resolve private Route 53 names for VPC services, and VPC workloads need to resolve on-premises names. What should be evaluated?
constraints: DNS queries must use controlled paths.

options.text: Evaluate Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules, on-premises resolver reachability, security groups, and query failure behavior.
Publish all private names in public DNS so both networks can resolve them.
Use a VPN route table to translate DNS names into IP addresses.
Assume VPC DNS automatically answers every on-premises private zone without forwarding configuration.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid DNS needs explicit resolver endpoints and forwarding rules across the network boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 Resolver endpoints receive or forward DNS queries through ENIs and rules to selected name servers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect places endpoints across AZs, restricts ports, and tests both directions and outage behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Public DNS exposes private names, routes do not translate names, and VPC DNS does not automatically know on-premises zones.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Resolver endpoints add ENIs and management but preserve private namespace ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private names and addresses should not be published publicly by default.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Routing forwards packets; it does not translate DNS names.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cross-network DNS requires endpoint and forwarding configuration.

items.prompt: A VPN reports connected tunnels but application requests still fail intermittently. Which signals should be correlated?
constraints: BGP or static routes are configured.

options.text: Correlate tunnel state, route advertisements, packet loss, bytes, NAT or firewall behavior, MTU, flow logs, and application latency instead of treating tunnel-up as end-to-end health.
Assume a connected IPSec tunnel proves every application port and return route work.
Restart both tunnels on every request to refresh their state.
Open all ports to the internet because VPN tunnel state is only a security label.

feedback.Reason: Tunnel establishment is only one layer; routing, filtering, MTU, and application behavior can still fail.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: VPN status reflects tunnel negotiation and may not prove prefix reachability, port access, return paths, or payload delivery.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator traces a test flow in both directions and fixes the first failed layer.
Details.errorCorrection: Connected does not mean application healthy, restarting is disruptive, and public open ports defeat private controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layered telemetry takes effort but avoids misdiagnosing a healthy tunnel as a healthy service path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Tunnel state does not validate routes or application ports.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Repeated restarts increase outage risk and hide the cause.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPN traffic should remain restricted to required private paths.

items.prompt: A Direct Connect route should be primary, with VPN as backup for the same on-premises prefix. What routing policy should be designed?

options.text: Set explicit BGP preference or path attributes so Direct Connect is preferred and VPN is retained as a tested backup, with symmetric return and convergence alarms.
Advertise identical routes and assume the lower-cost circuit is always selected as intended.
Remove the VPN route so failover cannot create an asymmetric path.
Use DNS priority because network prefixes are selected by hostname order.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid active-primary designs need explicit route preference and a tested backup path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: BGP attributes and AWS route selection determine which path is preferred; return routes must converge consistently.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner simulates circuit loss and verifies application recovery, route withdrawal, and restoration behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Equal advertisements may not produce the desired policy, removing backup defeats resilience, and DNS does not choose IP prefixes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping VPN warm costs resources but reduces recovery time when Direct Connect fails.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Route preference requires explicit policy and is not a generic circuit price rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing the backup path prevents the desired failover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS names do not determine BGP prefix selection.

items.prompt: A Direct Connect maintenance event can interrupt a critical data path. What availability measure should be added?
constraints: The workload has a strict RTO.

options.text: Maintain an independent VPN or second Direct Connect path, configure route failover, and rehearse maintenance and restoration rather than relying only on provider notice.
Assume a single Direct Connect circuit never has planned or unplanned interruption.
Disable BGP so a stale Direct Connect route remains primary during maintenance.
Increase application timeouts until the circuit returns without changing routing.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid availability needs an independent path and route behavior that can carry traffic during circuit maintenance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Direct Connect circuits and virtual interfaces can be unavailable during provider or facility events; route convergence determines backup use.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests failover and return-to-primary without duplicate sessions or route loops.
Details.errorCorrection: Provider notice is not continuity, stale routes can blackhole traffic, and timeouts do not provide a network path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backup connectivity costs more but converts a circuit event into a controlled degradation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Dedicated circuits still have maintenance and failure events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Stale primary routes can prevent safe failover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application waiting is not a network redundancy mechanism.

items.prompt: An enterprise advertises a broad summary route over Direct Connect and accidentally sends unrelated VPC traffic on premises. What should change?
constraints: The intended route set is documented.

options.text: Filter and summarize only intended prefixes, use route policies per environment or gateway, and verify forward and return paths with route inspection.
Advertise 0.0.0.0/0 everywhere because broad routes simplify operations safely.
Use security groups to prevent the route from being advertised.
Add more VIFs without changing advertisements or route domains.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid route advertisements define reachability and need least-privilege scope like other network controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: BGP and gateway route propagation can expose prefixes to connected networks; filters and route domains constrain the path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect publishes only required ranges and tests that disallowed destinations have no route.
Details.errorCorrection: Default routes can create unintended transit, security groups do not advertise routes, and more VIFs do not correct a policy error.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Summarization reduces route count but must not include destinations that should remain isolated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad default advertisements can create unintended routing and security exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are not BGP prefix filters.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Additional interfaces do not fix incorrect advertisements or route domains.

items.prompt: A Direct Connect path is private but the application requires encryption in transit for sensitive records. What should be evaluated?
constraints: The link is not itself an application encryption guarantee.
The application supports TLS or IPsec.

options.text: Use application or network-layer encryption over Direct Connect where required, manage keys and certificates, and measure overhead, MTU, inspection, and failover behavior.
Assume Direct Connect makes every application payload encrypted automatically.
Disable TLS because the circuit is not connected to the public internet.
Use a public VIF as the encryption mechanism for private records.

feedback.Reason: Direct Connect provides a private network path but does not automatically encrypt application payloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Encryption requirements are implemented by TLS, IPsec, or service-specific controls independent of physical or logical path privacy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses the encryption layer and tests certificate, key, MTU, performance, and recovery behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Private connectivity and encryption are distinct, disabling TLS violates the requirement, and public VIF is not a private-record protection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Encryption adds CPU and packet overhead but may be mandatory for confidentiality and compliance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct Connect is private connectivity, not universal payload encryption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private path does not remove application confidentiality requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VIF type does not itself provide application encryption.

items.prompt: A branch sends only a small number of requests but needs private access to several VPC services. What should be compared?

options.text: Compare Site-to-Site VPN with Direct Connect and centralized Transit Gateway routing using setup time, encryption, bandwidth, route scale, resilience, and cost for the actual traffic.
Choose Direct Connect solely because private circuits are always cheaper for low traffic.
Create a separate VPC peering connection from the branch to every service VPC without a VPN or DX gateway.
Use public endpoints and rely on application passwords as the hybrid network design.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid service selection balances bandwidth, latency, route scale, security, lead time, resilience, and total cost.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: VPN and Direct Connect have different provisioning, path, throughput, encryption, and gateway integration characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses a coherent hub and backup path rather than selecting from a single attribute.
Details.errorCorrection: Private circuits can be uneconomic at low volume, peering is VPC-to-VPC and not a branch path, and public endpoints change the security boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: VPN may be sufficient for modest traffic while Direct Connect is justified by predictable scale or policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct Connect economics include port, provider, and operations cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A branch needs a hybrid termination and scalable route design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public access is not equivalent to private hybrid connectivity.

items.prompt: After a circuit failure, traffic does not move to the VPN for several minutes. What should be investigated?
constraints: The application has a recovery objective.

options.text: Measure BGP withdrawal and advertisement timers, route preference, tunnel readiness, propagation, firewall state, and application retry behavior, then tune supported convergence controls.
Add DNS records because BGP convergence is controlled by hostname resolution.
Keep the failed route advertised so clients continue trying the primary path.
Increase application retry count without checking whether the backup route is usable.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid failover is an end-to-end convergence sequence involving routing, tunnel readiness, stateful controls, and clients.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: BGP route withdrawal and VPN tunnel establishment or propagation determine when a backup path is selected; clients may retain connections.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner rehearses link loss and restoration and aligns routing timers with application retry and RTO.
Details.errorCorrection: DNS does not control BGP route choice, failed route advertisements can blackhole traffic, and retries cannot fix an unusable backup.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Faster convergence can increase route churn or false failover and needs testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: BGP route selection is independent of DNS hostnames.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A failed primary route must withdraw or lose preference for backup traffic to flow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application retries need a reachable and correctly routed backup path.

items.prompt: A hybrid connection has a high circuit utilization average but periodic application timeouts. Which telemetry is needed?

options.text: Correlate utilization percentiles, packet loss, retransmission, queueing, tunnel or BGP state, per-service throughput, MTU, and application latency during bursts.
Use only the monthly average utilization because bursts cannot affect a provisioned circuit.
Increase the circuit immediately without checking packet loss or a single noisy service.
Disable alarms because Direct Connect and VPN are managed services.

feedback.Reason: Intermittent timeouts can be caused by burst, loss, MTU, route, or noisy-neighbor behavior hidden by averages.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Bandwidth and link state metrics must be correlated with packet and application signals to identify queue or path failure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator isolates the service or hop causing the issue before resizing or rerouting the entire hybrid fabric.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages hide bursts, immediate circuit expansion may not fix loss or MTU, and managed service status does not remove monitoring responsibility.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More telemetry enables targeted capacity changes and route policy but requires aggregation across providers and AWS metrics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Bursts and queues can cause timeouts even when averages look safe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity may not be the constrained dimension.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed connectivity still needs end-to-end operational monitoring.

items.prompt: A hybrid proposal says only that it needs a private connection and does not define bandwidth, encryption, RTO, routes, or failure domains. What should the architecture review require?
constraints: Some traffic is bursty and some sustained.

options.text: Define traffic volume and SLOs, VPN or Direct Connect fit, encryption, route domains, DNS, MTU, bandwidth headroom, physical diversity, failover, monitoring, and total cost before selecting the path.
Choose Direct Connect because every private connection has the same performance and resilience properties.
Choose VPN because encryption alone guarantees the required availability and throughput.
Add both services without route preference, ownership, or tested failure behavior.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid connectivity is a system design covering path, policy, capacity, and operations rather than a single product choice.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: VPN and Direct Connect differ in provisioning, path, throughput, route, encryption, failure, and cost behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses a primary and backup path with explicit route and test evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct Connect is not identical for every workload, VPN encryption does not guarantee bandwidth, and two ungoverned paths can create loops or asymmetry.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A coherent hybrid design may use both services when the RTO and bandwidth justify the added cost and operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct Connect performance and resilience depend on circuit and gateway design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: VPN encryption does not guarantee throughput or availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Multiple paths need explicit preference, ownership, and failure testing.
